gloss: To be formally in charge of a meeting, ceremony, or court.
examples: Judge Alvarez will *preside* at the hearing on Monday.
She *presided* over the committee for eight years.
The bishop has *presided* at every ordination since 2015.
contrast: Always takes *over* or *at*: *preside over a meeting*, never *preside a meeting*.

gloss: To keep the air or fluid inside something at a controlled pressure.
examples: Engineers *pressurize* the cabin so passengers can breathe at altitude.
The crew *pressurized* the airlock before opening the inner door.
The tank is *pressurized* to about thirty pounds per square inch.
contrast: In American English you *pressure* a person (*they pressured him to resign*) but *pressurize* a cabin or a tank.

gloss: To take something as true from the start, as the basis of an argument or plan.
examples: The whole plan *presupposes* that the funding is approved.
His question *presupposed* that I had already read the report.
Fair play cannot simply be *presupposed*; it has to be enforced.

gloss: To avoid telling the plain truth by speaking evasively.
examples: Answer the question and do not *prevaricate*.
The witness *prevaricated* for twenty minutes.
He was still *prevaricating* when the hearing ended.

gloss: To make a small hole in something with a sharp point.
examples: *Prick* the potatoes with a fork before baking them.
She *pricked* her finger on a thorn.
The nurse has already *pricked* his thumb for the blood test.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the wool prickled my neck*), intransitive (*my skin prickled*)
gloss: To cause or feel a light stinging, tingling sensation on the skin.
examples: Cheap wool sweaters *prickle* if you wear them next to the skin.
The cold air *prickled* her cheeks.
His scalp was *prickling* with sweat.

gloss: To be proud of a quality or achievement of your own.
examples: They *pride* themselves on answering every email within a day.
She *prided* herself on never missing a deadline.
He has always *prided* himself on his memory for names.
contrast: Only reflexive, and always with *on*: *pride yourself on something*, never *I pride my work*.

gloss: To prepare something or someone in advance so that it is ready to work or respond.
examples: *Prime* the wall before you paint it.
The lawyer *primed* her client for the cross-examination.
The pump has to be *primed* with water before it will draw.

gloss: To value something very highly.
examples: Collectors *prize* early editions of the book.
She *prized* her grandmother's ring above everything else she owned.
Quiet competence is *prized* at this company.
contrast: British writing also uses *prise* for forcing something open; American English writes *pry* for that.

gloss: To announce something publicly and with emphasis.
examples: The mayor will *proclaim* Saturday a day of remembrance.
He *proclaimed* himself the winner before the votes were counted.
Independence was *proclaimed* on the radio that morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (*procreate offspring*), intransitive (*pandas rarely procreate in captivity*)
gloss: To produce young.
examples: Pandas rarely *procreate* in captivity.
The pair *procreated* twice in five years.
The colony is *procreating* faster than the biologists expected.

gloss: To obtain something, especially with effort or through official channels.
examples: The agency *procures* uniforms for the whole department.
He *procured* a visa in less than a week.
Most of the equipment was *procured* from local suppliers.

gloss: To claim something openly, often when the claim may not be sincere.
examples: Candidates *profess* concern about housing every election year.
She *professed* to know nothing about the transfer.
He has *professed* his innocence from the first day.

gloss: To offer something formally, holding it out for the other side to accept.
examples: Witnesses may *proffer* documents to the court.
She *proffered* her hand, and he shook it.
No explanation has been *proffered* by the company.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: *proffered*, *proffering*.

gloss: To make an unfair profit out of a shortage or a crisis.
examples: Some sellers *profiteer* whenever there is a shortage.
Contractors *profiteered* during the reconstruction.
Companies accused of *profiteering* were called before Congress.

ru: быстро распространяться, расти в числе; размножаться
gloss: To increase quickly in number and spread widely.
examples: Delivery apps *proliferate* in every big city.
Rumors *proliferated* in the hours after the announcement.
Cheap drones have *proliferated* over the past decade.

gloss: To put a law or rule into effect by announcing it officially.
examples: Agencies *promulgate* rules only after a public comment period.
The council *promulgated* the new building code in March.
The standards were *promulgated* without much debate.

gloss: To support something by leaning it against a surface or placing a support under it.
examples: *Prop* the door open with that brick.
He *propped* his bike against the fence.
Her chin was *propped* on both hands.
contrast: Short vowel, so the p doubles: *propped*, *propping*.

gloss: To drive something forward.
examples: Two small motors *propel* the boat.
The scandal *propelled* her into national politics.
The craft is *propelled* by the solar wind.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: *propelled*, *propelling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he prophesied a crash*), intransitive (*she prophesies for a living*)
gloss: To say what will happen in the future, especially as an inspired prediction.
examples: Analysts *prophesy* a hard winter for retailers.
He *prophesied* the collapse two years before it came.
Everything she had *prophesied* came true.
contrast: The verb *prophesy* ends in -sy and rhymes with *sigh*; the noun *prophecy* ends in -cy and rhymes with *see*.

gloss: To divide or charge an amount in proportion to the time or share actually used.
examples: We *prorate* the rent if you move in mid-month.
The airline *prorated* the refund for the unused leg.
Your first bill will be *prorated* from the day of installation.

gloss: To forbid something officially.
examples: Federal law *proscribes* discrimination in hiring.
The regime *proscribed* every opposition party.
Several additives are *proscribed* in baby food.
contrast: *Proscribe* means forbid; *prescribe* means order or recommend. A doctor *prescribes* a drug, a law *proscribes* it.

ru: обращать в свою веру, проповедовать; вербовать сторонников
transitivity: both — transitive (*they proselytized the whole village*), intransitive (*volunteers are told not to proselytize*)
gloss: To try to persuade people to join your religion or adopt your beliefs.
examples: Volunteers are told to help, not to *proselytize*.
He *proselytized* door to door for two years.
Staff complained about a colleague *proselytizing* at work.

gloss: To search an area for gold, oil, or minerals, or in sales to search for new customers.
examples: Crews still *prospect* for lithium in the desert.
His great-grandfather *prospected* for gold in Alaska.
The team spent the winter *prospecting* for new clients.
contrast: Takes *for*: *prospect for gold*, not *prospect gold*.

gloss: To do well, especially in money or business.
examples: Small shops *prosper* when the street is busy.
The family *prospered* after the war.
The company has *prospered* under new management.

gloss: To make something last longer than it needs to.
examples: Do not *protract* the meeting with side questions.
Appeals *protracted* the case for six years.
The dispute has been *protracted* by both sides.

gloss: To stick out from a surface.
examples: Rusty nails *protrude* from the old fence.
A rock *protruded* through the snow.
Wires were *protruding* from the wall.

gloss: To examine someone's mind and motives by the methods of psychoanalysis, or informally to pick apart their behavior.
examples: Please do not *psychoanalyze* me at dinner.
The book *psychoanalyzed* three famous painters.
He spent the whole drive home *psychoanalyzing* his boss.
contrast: The p is silent. American spelling is *psychoanalyze*; British writing uses *psychoanalyse*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she puckered her lips*), intransitive (*the seam puckered*)
gloss: To draw skin or cloth into small tight folds.
examples: Lemons make you *pucker* your lips.
The seam *puckered* after the first wash.
She was *puckering* her forehead at the screen.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the chimney puffed smoke*), intransitive (*he puffed up the stairs*)
gloss: To blow out air or smoke in short bursts, or to breathe hard.
examples: The old engines still *puff* smoke over the valley.
He *puffed* on a cigar between innings.
She arrived *puffing* after six flights of stairs.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he puked up his lunch*), intransitive (*the dog puked on the rug*)
gloss: To vomit.
examples: Kids on that ride often *puke*.
The dog *puked* on the rug again.
He has been *puking* since midnight.
contrast: Very informal. *Vomit* is the neutral word, and *throw up* the everyday one.

gloss: To expand and contract, or grow strong and weak, in a steady rhythm.
examples: The lights *pulsate* in time with the music.
His whole hand *pulsated* with pain.
The floor was *pulsating* from the bass.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the laser pulses light into the fiber*), intransitive (*blood pulses through the vessels*)
gloss: To beat or move in a steady rhythm.
examples: Blood *pulses* through the vessels with every heartbeat.
The music *pulsed* through the floor.
A red light was *pulsing* on the dashboard.

gloss: To crush something into powder, or to defeat it completely.
examples: The mill *pulverizes* the rock before it is washed.
The storm *pulverized* the old pier.
Their defense was *pulverized* in the second half.

transitivity: both — transitive (*pump water from the well*), intransitive (*his heart was pumping hard*)
gloss: To move liquid or air with a pump, or to move something with that same in-and-out motion.
examples: These wells *pump* water all summer.
He *pumped* the brakes on the icy road.
Millions of gallons are being *pumped* into the reservoir.

gloss: To blend food into a smooth, thick paste.
examples: *Puree* the soup in batches so it does not splash.
She *pureed* the carrots for the baby.
The sauce is made by *pureeing* roasted peppers.
contrast: Both e's stay before the ending: *pureed*, *pureeing*.

gloss: To get rid of people or things that are considered unwanted.
examples: New owners often *purge* the old management team.
The party *purged* its critics after the vote.
Old records were *purged* from the database.

gloss: To remove dirt or harmful substances from something.
examples: Charcoal filters *purify* the water in an hour.
They *purified* the sample twice before testing it.
The air is *purified* before it reaches the lab.
contrast: The -y becomes -ie in *purifies* and *purified*, but stays in *purifying*.

gloss: To claim to be or do something, especially when the claim may be false.
examples: The emails *purport* to come from the bank.
The film *purported* to be a true story.
A document *purporting* to show the payment was leaked.
contrast: The verb is stressed pur-PORT and is followed by *to* plus a verb; the noun *purport* (meaning) is stressed PUR-port.

gloss: To draw your lips together into a tight round shape.
examples: Some people *purse* their lips when they concentrate.
She *pursed* her mouth and said nothing.
He listened with *pursed* lips.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the city quadrupled its bus fleet*), intransitive (*prices quadrupled*)
gloss: To become four times as large, or to make something four times as large.
examples: Prices could *quadruple* if the harvest fails.
The city *quadrupled* its bus fleet in a decade.
Enrollment has *quadrupled* since 2010.

ru: измерять, определять количественно; оценивать в цифрах
gloss: To measure something and express it as a number.
examples: It is hard to *quantify* the damage to the brand.
Researchers *quantified* the effect at about nine percent.
The benefits have never been properly *quantified*.
contrast: The -y becomes -ie in *quantifies* and *quantified*, but stays in *quantifying*.

ru: делить на четыре части, разрезать на четвертинки
gloss: To cut something into four pieces.
examples: *Quarter* the apples and cut out the cores.
He *quartered* the pizza with a wheel cutter.
The chicken is sold whole or *quartered*.

ru: ставить в очередь, выстраиваться в очередь
transitivity: both — transitive (*I queued three episodes*), intransitive (*shoppers queued outside*)
gloss: To line up, or to put items in a line so they are handled one after another.
examples: Downloads *queue* automatically when the network is slow.
I *queued* three episodes for the flight.
Shoppers were *queuing* outside before dawn.
contrast: Five letters, one sound: KYOO. The -ing form is written *queuing* or *queueing*; both are accepted.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she quickened her pace*), intransitive (*his pulse quickened*)
gloss: To become faster, or to make something faster.
examples: His steps *quicken* whenever he passes that dog.
She *quickened* her pace to catch the bus.
Interest in the case is *quickening* again.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he quipped that it could have been an email*), intransitive (*she quipped back*)
gloss: To say something clever and funny, usually in reply.
examples: He can *quip* his way out of any interview.
She *quipped* that the meeting could have been an email.
A reporter *quipping* about the delay got the biggest laugh.
contrast: Short vowel, so the p doubles: *quipped*, *quipping*.

gloss: To shake with small, rapid movements.
examples: Her hands *quiver* when she is nervous.
The arrow *quivered* in the target.
His voice was *quivering* by the end of the speech.

gloss: To cause someone sharp physical or mental pain.
examples: Doubts *rack* him every time he has to decide.
A coughing fit *racked* her whole body.
He has been *racking* his brain for the name all morning.
contrast: In *rack your brain* the spelling is *rack*, not *wrack*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the crackdown radicalized a generation*), intransitive (*the movement radicalized quickly*)
gloss: To make someone adopt extreme political or religious views, or to become that way.
examples: Recruiters try to *radicalize* teenagers online.
The crackdown *radicalized* a whole generation.
He was *radicalized* during his first year abroad.

ru: передавать по радио, радировать; связаться по рации
transitivity: both — transitive (*radio the base*), intransitive (*he radioed for help*)
gloss: To send a message by radio.
examples: Pilots *radio* the tower before landing.
The captain *radioed* for help at midnight.
They were *radioing* their position every hour.
contrast: No -y change and no extra e: *radios*, *radioed*, *radioing*.

gloss: To continue with great force, or to show violent anger.
examples: Wildfires *rage* through the canyon every fall.
The debate *raged* for three hours.
A storm has been *raging* off the coast since Tuesday.

gloss: To complain about something angrily and at length.
examples: Columnists *rail* against the tax every spring.
He *railed* at the referee for ten minutes.
She has been *railing* against the decision all week.
contrast: Takes *against* or *at*: *rail against the rules*, never *rail the rules*.

gloss: To force something through, or force someone into a decision, without proper discussion.
examples: Do not let them *railroad* you into signing anything.
The committee *railroaded* the proposal through in one night.
Many believe he was *railroaded* by a rushed trial.

transitivity: both — transitive (*a truck rammed the barrier*), intransitive (*the boat rammed into the dock*)
gloss: To hit or push something with great force.
examples: Tugboats *ram* the ice to keep the channel open.
A truck *rammed* the barrier at the gate.
The post had been *rammed* two feet into the ground.
contrast: Short vowel, so the m doubles: *rammed*, *ramming*.

gloss: To talk or write at length without a clear point.
examples: I *ramble* when I am nervous.
He *rambled* for twenty minutes about parking.
She kept *rambling* until someone changed the subject.

gloss: To rush about violently, causing damage.
examples: Elephants sometimes *rampage* through the fields at night.
Fans *rampaged* through the streets after the loss.
A bear was *rampaging* through the campground.
contrast: The verb is stressed ram-PAYJ; the noun *a rampage* is stressed RAM-payj.

gloss: To put things in a random order, or assign them by chance.
examples: The app can *randomize* the play order.
Researchers *randomized* patients into two groups.
The questions are *randomized* for every student.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the comment rankled him*), intransitive (*the decision still rankles*)
gloss: To keep causing annoyance or resentment long after the event.
examples: Small slights *rankle* for years.
The comment *rankled* him all evening.
The pay gap is still *rankling* with staff.

gloss: To search a place roughly, leaving it in disorder, usually in order to steal.
examples: Thieves *ransack* empty houses during vacation season.
Someone *ransacked* the office over the weekend.
Every drawer had been *ransacked*.

gloss: To speak or write angrily and at length.
examples: He will *rant* about the parking for an hour.
She *ranted* at the customer service desk.
Someone was *ranting* outside the courthouse.
contrast: Usually with *about* or *at*: *rant about the fees*, *rant at the staff*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he rationalized the lie*), intransitive (*we all rationalize*)
gloss: To invent reasonable-sounding explanations for behavior that is not reasonable.
examples: People *rationalize* almost any purchase.
He *rationalized* the lie as protecting his family.
She has *rationalized* every missed deadline this year.
contrast: American spelling is *rationalize*; British writing uses *rationalise*.

gloss: To talk about something with great enthusiasm.
examples: Critics *rave* about her second novel.
He *raved* about the tacos the whole drive home.
Everyone is *raving* about the new season.
contrast: Takes *about* or *over*: *rave about the food*.

gloss: To act or feel in response to something that has happened.
examples: Markets *react* badly to uncertainty.
She *reacted* calmly to the news.
The crowd was *reacting* to something we could not see.
contrast: Takes *to*: *react to the decision*, never *react the decision*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he readjusted the mirror*), intransitive (*your eyes readjust slowly*)
gloss: To change something again, or to get used to a situation again after a change.
examples: Give your eyes a minute to *readjust* to the dark.
He *readjusted* the mirror before pulling out.
The family is still *readjusting* after the move.

gloss: To prepare someone or something for what is coming.
examples: Crews *ready* the plows before the first storm.
She *readied* herself for bad news.
The team is *readying* a response for the morning.
contrast: The -y becomes -ie in *readies* and *readied*, but stays in *readying*.

gloss: To state again that something is still true or still your position.
examples: Both sides *reaffirm* the ceasefire every year.
The court *reaffirmed* its earlier ruling.
Support for the program has been *reaffirmed* in writing.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the shop realigned the wheels*), intransitive (*the parties realigned after the vote*)
gloss: To put something into a new position or arrangement.
examples: The shop can *realign* the front wheels in an hour.
The merger *realigned* the whole industry.
Districts are being *realigned* after the census.
contrast: The g is silent: ree-uh-LYN.

gloss: To give money, staff, or space to a different purpose than before.
examples: We can *reallocate* the unused budget.
The school *reallocated* two classrooms to the art program.
Funds have been *reallocated* to emergency housing.

gloss: To be seen again after being absent.
examples: The symptoms usually *reappear* in cold weather.
He *reappeared* an hour later with coffee for everyone.
The file has *reappeared* in the trash folder.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he reassembled the engine*), intransitive (*the class reassembled outside*)
gloss: To put something back together, or for a group to gather again.
examples: Label the parts so you can *reassemble* the shelf.
The class *reassembled* on the field after the fire drill.
The engine was *reassembled* in a single day.

gloss: To give someone a different job or post, or to give a task to someone else.
examples: Managers can *reassign* cases at any point.
The officer was *reassigned* to desk duty.
They are *reassigning* half the team to the new project.
contrast: The g is silent: ree-uh-SYN.

transitivity: both — transitive (*we rebooked the room*), intransitive (*passengers had to rebook online*)
gloss: To arrange a new booking after the first one is canceled or changed.
examples: The agent can *rebook* you on the morning flight.
We *rebooked* the room for October.
Thousands of passengers are still being *rebooked*.

ru: проводить ребрендинг, менять название и образ
transitivity: both — transitive (*they rebranded the chain*), intransitive (*the airline rebranded last year*)
gloss: To give a company or product a new name and image.
examples: Struggling chains often *rebrand* rather than close.
The airline *rebranded* after the merger.
The store has been *rebranded* twice in five years.

gloss: To reject an offer or approach in a blunt, unfriendly way.
examples: Regulators regularly *rebuff* requests like this one.
She *rebuffed* every attempt to settle.
His offer was *rebuffed* within the hour.

gloss: To argue with evidence that a claim or accusation is wrong.
examples: The defense will *rebut* each charge in turn.
She *rebutted* the figures with data of her own.
The central claim has never been *rebutted*.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the t doubles: *rebutted*, *rebutting*.
